name: Galle
line: A walled fort town on the south coast, best after the day-trippers leave.

image.alt: A lit café street inside Galle Fort at night

summary: A walled fort town on the south coast. Busy at midday, quiet and golden by evening, and still lived in.

intro.heading: A fort that is still a town.
paragraphs: Galle Fort was begun by the Portuguese and rebuilt by the Dutch in the seventeenth century. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site now, but people still live, work and go to school inside the walls, and that is what makes it worth staying in rather than passing through.
Most visitors come on a day trip from the beaches and leave by late afternoon. We book a night or two inside the walls, so you have the ramparts at sunset and the lanes to yourself in the morning.

mapCaption: On the south western corner of the island. The other dots are the places we pair it with.

doing.lede: Galle is best taken slowly. These are the things we build the days around.

items.title: The ramparts at sunset
items.body: Walk the walls from the clock tower round to the lighthouse as the light goes. Half the town does the same, and it never feels crowded.

items.title: The lanes before breakfast
items.body: Churches, a mosque, old Dutch houses and the first cafés opening, while the streets are still being swept.

items.title: A day on the nearby beaches
items.body: Unawatuna and the quieter coves beyond it are a short drive east when you want to swim.

items.title: Dinner inside the walls
items.body: Restaurants in restored houses, all a few minutes’ walk from wherever you are staying.

gallery.alt: A lone walker on an empty stretch of the south coast
A table set on the sand as a couple walk the beach

season: Galle follows the south and west coast: dry and calm from December to April, wet while the south west monsoon blows from May to September. Whales pass Mirissa, a short drive east, from November to April.
ctaBody: Tell us your dates and we will fit it in, with a room inside the walls.
